title: Adelaide's stalled Aboriginal cultural centre has a dubious future on a site with a troubled past.

An artist's impression of the Lot Fourteen site, with the proposed Tarrkarri gallery on the right. (Supplied: SA government)

The South Australian public has known since 2007 that the old Royal Adelaide Hospital site on North Terrace would one day become vacant.

And yet, nearly 20 years on, it is still in the dark about what will replace it.

That such a prime parcel of land on Adelaide's cultural boulevard could be subject to this level of inaction can reasonably be interpreted as an extraordinary failure of urban planning.

The latest proposal — an Aboriginal cultural centre potentially costing up to $600 million — has now been on hold for three-and-a-half years, its spot at Lot Fourteen still just a hole in the ground.

The construction of Tarrkarri on North Terrace in Adelaide CBD has halted.  (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Tarrkarri means "the future" in Kaurna language, but understanding the project's troubles requires a deep dive into the past.

Some argue it's time to ponder whether it was even a good idea in the first place.

The stasis at the old RAH site started well before Tarrkarri, and it's not been for a lack of ideas about what to put there.

The Rann Labor government got the ball rolling in 2007, suggesting much of the land could be returned to the adjacent Botanic Gardens while some of the heritage buildings could be repurposed into museums or galleries.

Six years later, the Weatherill government opened an international design competition that attracted more than 120 entries and a lot of press.

A Slovakian studio's vision for an artificial green mountain made from the old hospital's debris didn't make the final cut, nor did a local architect's bid for a 280-metre-tall observation tower.

The eventual winner — a Victorian architect's $300 million proposal for a school, student accommodation building and art gallery — was quietly ignored anyway.

As the visions of utopia piled up, the clock was running down on the hospital's relocation.

One of the proposals involved an artificial mountain. (Supplied: Nice architects + Mulloway studio)

A prescient cabinet document from May 2014, obtained by the ABC via Freedom of Information, warned ministers that the "risks of inaction are substantial" given the city's East End would face an economic hit when the hospital left.

"Plans must be well enough advanced that 'downtime' following the relocation of hospital functions is minimised," the cabinet note said.

A $1 billion deal for a private consortium to build a luxury precinct on the vacant Royal Adelaide Hospital site falls through, with the SA government to take charge and offer student accommodation and a gallery of modern art in a downsized project.

The Weatherill government then spent a year in negotiations with developers Commercial and General for a $1 billion "24-hour city" featuring a luxury hotel, arts and culture precinct and more than 1,000 apartments.

Those negotiations broke down in September 2017 — just two weeks after the hospital's exit — leaving the government to take over management of the site and insist it wasn't back at square one.

But its new plan included returning 30 per cent of the land to the Botanic Gardens — almost identical to what was proposed back in 2007.

Labor was swept from power in March 2018, but not before it could launch another international competition for the old RAH site.

This time it was to design a new contemporary art gallery — architecturally on par with Hobart's MONA or Bilbao's Guggenheim — to give the Art Gallery of SA a space to exhibit its modern collection, which is mostly in storage.

An architect's $300 million proposal for a school, student accommodation building and art gallery won a 2013 design competition. (Supplied: Slash Architects)

But when the newly elected Marshall government inherited the winning designs in mid-2018, it tasked the successful architects with drawing up an Aboriginal art and culture gallery instead. The Liberal Party had promised one before the election.

The final $200 million plan was bigger than the SA Museum and Art Gallery combined — "the most impressive building on the South Australian skyline", then-Premier Steven Marshall proclaimed — designed for exhibitions, performances and the display of tens of thousands of Indigenous artefacts currently in storage.

Construction on Tarrkarri began in December 2021, but the Liberals lost the state election four months later.

The Malinauskas government then halted works in October 2022, citing a $50 million cost blowout and advice that the centre would only be of state-level significance. A subsequent project review found an internationally significant centre could cost up to $600 million to build.

Tarrkarri remains on hold today, with the government's efforts to make up the $400 million gap via philanthropic or extra Commonwealth money falling short.

But Premier Peter Malinauskas has remained supportive of the Tarrkarri vision, despite not putting in more state funding.

"While some people's appetite for this project might have diminished in recent years, in some ways I see the merit for it going up," he said last month.

Others, however, are arguing for a complete rethink.

Among those is Adelaide art historian and curator Margot Osborne, who believes the old vision for a contemporary art gallery should be revisited.

A design submitted by Diller Scofidio + Renfro and Woods Bagot for the old Royal Adelaide Hospital site. (Supplied)

Dr Osborne highlighted that Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane all have modern galleries, while Adelaide has "a very strong collection that at present isn't adequately displayed".

"It is a risk to spend $600 million — if that's the actual price — on something that has never been tested," she said.

Prominent art critic John McDonald agrees, arguing a contemporary gallery could still host a substantial amount of Indigenous work.

He also questions whether Tarrkarri would be able to differentiate itself from other Indigenous gallery projects across the country or display artefacts that attract repeat visitation.

"Most of the great Aboriginal works, most of the works by sensational artists, are already in public collections or in top private collections," he said.

Plans for Tarrkarri included exhibition and performance spaces, terraced landscapes, and a gathering area for cultural ceremonies. (Supplied: Woods Bagot)

Mr McDonald, a former head of Australian art at the National Gallery of Australia, said there will be backlash for changing course but it's time to "bite the bullet".

"Because this project, as it stands, is unrealisable.

"At some stage someone has to step in and say okay enough is enough, this is going nowhere.

"There are interest groups that are going to be angry … but you have to face them down and do what is the proper thing for everybody."

There are political risks proceeding with Tarrkarri as planned too.

The Malinauskas government is operating in a post Voice referendum environment where One Nation is the state's second-highest polling party. A $600 million Indigenous gallery will be ripe for the political charge of "wrong priorities".

"There's a general nervousness about investment, I think, in Aboriginal projects in the current political climate," said David Rathman, the former ambassador for the Tarrkarri project.

"I really find that at my age very disappointing."

David Rathman is the former ambassador for the Tarrkarri project.

The premier last month alluded to his fears Tarrkarri could become "hyper partisan" if it did not have Liberal Party support.

"[That would] have the impact of undermining the social licence for the project and in the process doing grave harm to the Indigenous community in this state that is still feeling the scars of the Voice debate," Mr Malinauskas said last month.

Former Premier Steven Marshall vowed when he took office that the old RAH would not "turn into another Le Cornu site" — a reference to an infamous plot of land in North Adelaide that remained vacant for more than 30 years.

The Le Cornu block at North Adelaide was infamously vacant for decades. (ABC News: Malcolm Sutton)

The site has partially avoided that fate. Several international technology companies are now based at Lot Fourteen, and a 12-storey "Innovation Centre" was last week granted planning approval.

But the precinct is still missing its cultural centrepiece.

Given no other piece of land is coming up on the cultural boulevard for the next 100 years, the stakes for Adelaide's arts sector could not be higher.

"There is a chance that we get this up but there is also a chance that we do not," Mr Malinauskas said of Tarrkarri.

"Clearly, at some point, the government will have to make a decision about whether or not we go with it or not.

"That time cannot be too far away."
